content: The Guidelines for the Management of Symptomatic Sexually Transmitted Infections were published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in June 2021. These guidelines aim to provide evidence-based recommendations for the clinical management of individuals presenting with symptoms of sexually transmitted infections (STIs). They are designed to assist healthcare providers and program managers in delivering high-quality STI care, particularly in resource-limited settings. In settings where same-day molecular testing is available, treatment should be based on test results provided during the same visit. If molecular testing is not feasible, syndromic management remains a recommended approach, ensuring immediate treatment for common infections based on clinical symptoms. For individuals with urethral discharge, the guidelines recommend molecular testing to identify N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis. If tests are negative, treatment should address other potential causes, such as Mycoplasma genitalium or Trichomonas vaginalis. In cases of recurrent or persistent urethral discharge, repeat molecular testing is advised, including testing for antimicrobial-resistant N. gonorrhoeae. For vaginal discharge, treatment should address N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, and T. vaginalis based on molecular test results. In the absence of testing, syndromic management should include treatment for bacterial vaginosis if clinical signs are present. A thorough medical and sexual history, along with a physical examination, is recommended to assess for pelvic inflammatory disease, pregnancy, or other conditions. In cases of lower abdominal pain in sexually active women, the guidelines suggest immediate treatment for pelvic inflammatory disease if clinical signs such as cervical motion tenderness or lower abdominal tenderness are present. Follow-up assessments should be scheduled to monitor clinical improvement. For genital ulcers, including anorectal ulcers, molecular testing of lesions is recommended to confirm or exclude infections such as herpes simplex virus (HSV) and syphilis (Treponema pallidum). In settings where molecular testing is unavailable, syndromic treatment should be provided, with adjustments made once test results become available. Treatment for lymphogranuloma venereum should be initiated if test results are positive. The guidelines also highlight the importance of partner notification and treatment to prevent reinfection and further transmission. These recommendations are intended to support countries in updating their national STI management guidelines and to serve as a resource for healthcare providers, policymakers, and stakeholders involved in STI prevention and care. The guidelines were developed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach, ensuring that recommendations are based on the best available evidence.
